problem.text: In $\triangle ABC$, $\overline{AC} = \overline{CD}$ and $\angle CAB - \angle ABC = 30^\circ$. What is $\angle BAD$?

steps.title: Where to start: the equal sides make an isosceles triangle
steps.body: The given $AC = CD$ is the clue: triangle $ACD$ is isosceles. Its base angles are equal, so call $\angle CAD = \angle CDA = x$. Also call the angle we want $\angle BAD = y$. Naming angles with letters turns the angle chase into a little algebra.

your_turn.prompt: Why are $\angle CAD$ and $\angle CDA$ equal?
your_turn.answer: They are opposite the equal sides $CD$ and $CA$ of triangle $ACD$.

steps.title: Use the $30^\circ$ condition
steps.body: Segment $AD$ splits $\angle CAB$ into two parts, so $\angle CAB = x + y$. The problem says $\angle CAB$ is $30^\circ$ more than $\angle ABC$, which lets us write $\angle ABC$ in terms of $x$ and $y$ too.

your_turn.prompt: Write $\angle ABC$ in terms of $x$ and $y$.

steps.title: Look at triangle $ABD$
steps.body: Triangle $ABD$ has angles $\angle BAD = y$ and $\angle ABD = x + y - 30^\circ$. Its third angle is at $D$. Since $D$ lies on segment $BC$, the angles $\angle CDA$ and $\angle BDA$ sit side by side on a straight line.

your_turn.answer: $180^\circ - x$, because it is supplementary to $\angle CDA = x$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: The angles of triangle $ABD$ add to $180^\circ$: $$y + (180 - x) + (x + y - 30) = 180.$$ The $x$ cancels, leaving $2y = 30$, so $y = 15$. That means $\angle BAD$ is the same no matter how the triangle is shaped. The answer is **$15^\circ$**.
